text: The name Bradford comes from a wide ford over the Avon, which flows westward through the parish. The crossing served routes running north and south, and the ford stayed in use alongside the later stone bridge until the nineteenth century.
source_title: Bradford on Avon (Community History)
source_author: Wiltshire and Swindon History Centre, Wiltshire Council
uncertainty: No named author. The writing date is inferred because the page treats 2002 as the present.

text: Town Bridge began in the 1200s as a packhorse crossing, possibly replacing an earlier bridge. Two of its original pointed, ribbed arches survive at the south end on the east side, and in 1400 the Pope supported an appeal for alms to pay for repairs.
source_title: The Town Bridge (List Entry 1036011)
uncertainty: The listing says an earlier bridge may have stood here. The RAI summary notes a bridge mentioned in the late 12th century, and Wiltshire Council says the first stone bridge was Norman.

text: A small square domed building on the bridge, probably of the 1600s, was used as the town lock-up in the eighteenth century and known as a blind house. A stone vault inside forms two cells, and its gilded copper fish weathervane, the Bradford Gudgeon, may be sixteenth-century.
source_title: The Town Bridge (List Entry 1036011)
uncertainty: The building's 17th-century date and the vane's 16th-century date are both given only as probable. Other sources say the lock-up replaced a medieval bridge chapel.

text: The bridge was only about ten feet wide until its width was doubled in 1768-9. The lock-up on its upstream side began as a medieval bridge chapel, which the antiquary John Aubrey noted on a visit, and was later rebuilt, perhaps to hold prisoners briefly.
source_title: Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire: archaeology and history (summer meeting notes)
source_author: Royal Archaeological Institute; town section by Pam and Ivor Slocombe
uncertainty: The widening date conflicts between sources. Historic England's listing places it in the 17th century, while this summary and the 2012 town trail give 1768-9 or 1769.

text: Barton Bridge is a fourteenth-century former packhorse bridge with four pointed arches reaching a small island, and three triangular cutwaters on its upstream face. A narrower footbridge over a side stream was added in the mid-1800s, and a Second World War pillbox stands on the island.
source_title: Barton Bridge (List Entry 1364494)
uncertainty: Documents suggest the cutwaters were added later in the medieval period. Many facing stones come from a late-19th-century repair.

text: The great barn was probably built in the 1330s for Barton Grange, the home farm of Shaftesbury Abbey, a very wealthy Dorset nunnery. The abbey acquired Bradford's rectory and its tithes in 1332, hence the tithe-barn label; a smaller barn about 43 metres long preceded it around 1300.
source_title: History of Bradford-on-Avon Tithe Barn
uncertainty: No document confirms the 1330s build date, and what the barn actually stored is unclear.

text: Shaftesbury Abbey held a large estate centred on Bradford from about 1001 through the Middle Ages, managed from Barton. Tree-ring dating places the great barn's two-tier cruck roof between 1334 and 1379, the barn was standing by 1367, and the nearby granary dates to 1370-90.
source_title: Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire: archaeology and history (summer meeting notes)
source_author: Royal Archaeological Institute; Barton Farm section by Pam and Ivor Slocombe
uncertainty: Tree-ring dating gives a range, not a single year, and the grant date is approximate.

text: William of Malmesbury saw the church standing in the 1120s and linked it to St Aldhelm, who died in 709. Its architecture instead points to building in the early eleventh century for the Shaftesbury nuns after the 1001 grant; its rich carving may relate to relics of Edward the Martyr.
source_title: Saxon Church of St Laurence
uncertainty: The dating is disputed. Medieval tradition favours Aldhelm c.700, current opinion the early 11th century, and Wiltshire Council's page says late 10th century. The link to relics is speculative.

text: Canon Jones of Holy Trinity identified the forgotten building in 1856 after reading William of Malmesbury. Other buildings had boxed it in, the chancel had been turned into a three-storey cottage, its arch replaced by a chimney built from the same stones, and an upper room held a school.
source_title: Church of St. Laurence, Bradford on Avon
uncertainty: The National Churches Trust says carved angels uncovered during repairs in 1856 led to the identification. One town website gives 1871 instead.

text: The council-backed visitor website says the Saxon Church of St Laurence dates from about AD 700 and was found only in 1871. It also says Saxons had reached the area by 652 and that the town grew around the river ford.
source_title: History of Bradford on Avon
source_author: Explore Bradford on Avon (Bradford on Avon Town Council)
uncertainty: An unattributed popular summary. It conflicts with the National Churches Trust, Wiltshire Council and the RAI, which favour a late 10th- or early 11th-century building rediscovered in 1856.

text: During 2016 renovation and flood-protection work at Holy Trinity, on the Avon's north bank, archaeologists found early burials under the boiler-house floor, one cut by the 12th-century nave. Radiocarbon dated two to roughly the 800s-900s, pointing to an earlier church, perhaps Aldhelm's minster of about 705.
source_title: New evidence for a lost church
uncertainty: The link between the burials and Aldhelm's minster is a hypothesis, and the radiocarbon results are broad ranges. The article treats St Laurence as almost certainly built after 1001.

text: In 652 Cenwalh, king of Wessex, fought a battle at a place recorded as Bradonforde be afne, the earliest written reference to the town. By 705 a small monastery headed by St Aldhelm stood on the north-west bank of the river.
source_title: Bradford on Avon (Community History)
source_author: Wiltshire and Swindon History Centre, Wiltshire Council
uncertainty: The battle site has not been located, and the RAI suggests it may have been Budbury hillfort. The monastery's position is inferred, not excavated.

text: Budbury holds an Iron Age hillfort, partly excavated by Geoffrey Wainwright in the late 1960s, that may have been reused after Roman rule. A twelfth-century text names a battle at Wirtgeornsburh, meaning Vortigern's fort, possibly the West Saxon-British fight of 652.
source_title: Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire: archaeology and history (summer meeting notes)
uncertainty: Identifying Wirtgeornsburh with Budbury, and with the 652 battle, is tentative. Sources disagree on the fort's size, giving about 6 or about 10 acres.

text: Teachers noticed lines of parched grass on St Laurence School's football pitch, matching buried walls. Excavations led by Mark Corney of Bristol University revealed two fourth-century Roman villas linked by a long corridor paved with a large mosaic of a vase between dolphins, probably made in Cirencester.
source_title: Mosaic news brief (Archaeology vol. 55 no. 6)
uncertainty: This report gives 40 rooms per villa and a 4th-century date. The 2003 Telegraph report dates the oldest parts to AD 230-270 and gives about 15 ground-floor rooms in the main villa.

text: After Roman rule ended, a round baptistery about 15 feet across was cut into the reception-room mosaic of the eastern villa in the fifth century. The excavators called it the earliest known private chapel in post-Roman Britain; the villas were occupied from the 230s into the fifth century.
source_title: Unearthed: a luxury Roman villa with chapel and granny flat (Daily Telegraph, reproduced on romanhideout.com)
uncertainty: The baptistery is an interpretation of a circular feature, and the RAI summary also presents it that way. This text is a copy on a secondary website.

text: Kingston Mill was built beside the Avon in 1807. In 1848 Stephen Moulton, who had bought the neighbouring Hall, turned the then-idle mill into a rubber factory. A textile mill close to the Hall drew its water through a leat channelled off the river.
source_title: Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire: archaeology and history (summer meeting notes)
source_author: Royal Archaeological Institute; town section by Pam and Ivor Slocombe
uncertainty: The summary does not name the mill fed by the leat or say when the leat was dug.

text: Moulton chose the disused Kingston woollen mills for rubber-making in 1848 because empty factories already fitted for water and steam power stood ready, along with workers used to mill life. Early products included buffers, springs and hoses for the Great Western Railway.
source_title: Engineering & Industry
source_author: Explore Bradford on Avon (Bradford on Avon Town Council)
uncertainty: Unattributed tourism text. It gives 1995 for the end of rubber production, while other sources give 1991-92.

text: The weir near Avoncliff aqueduct, downstream of the town, holds back about two metres of water, and a local book suggests it dates from the late 900s. In 2020 engineers judged a breach likely, which could lower levels up to Greenland Mills by one to two metres, prompting community-funded emergency repairs.
source_title: Avoncliff weir repairs supported by community
uncertainty: The 10th-century origin rests on one local history book by Trevor Turpin. The article does not confirm that the repairs were finished.

text: By the early 1500s Avoncliff had a mill on each bank of the Avon, grinding corn and fulling cloth. Around 1791 Moggeridge and Joyce installed water-driven cloth machinery there, perhaps the first locally; from the mid-1800s to the late 1930s both mills shredded old textiles into upholstery flock.
source_title: Westwood / Avoncliff (Community History)
uncertainty: The page says the c.1791 installation was possibly, not certainly, the earliest in the area.

text: Avoncliff Aqueduct, designed by John Rennie, carries the Kennet and Avon Canal over the river on three tall segmental arches, the middle one highest. The canal was closed and drained in 1954 and reopened after restoration in the 1980s; the aqueduct was listed Grade II* in 1988.
source_title: Kennet and Avon Canal, Avoncliff Aqueduct (List Entry 1021876)
uncertainty: The listing dates the aqueduct to c.1810, but Wiltshire Council's community history gives construction as 1795-98. The Kennet & Avon Canal Trust gives 1990 as the year the whole canal reopened.

text: The aqueduct's central arch sags slightly, possibly because supporting centring was removed before mortar set or because porous limestone was damaged by frost during building. After the Great Western Railway bought the canal in 1852, cracked stonework was patched with blue brick; the Canal & River Trust later repaired it in harder matching stone.
source_title: John Rennie's Dundas and Avoncliff aqueducts
uncertainty: The page offers two possible causes of the sag and does not settle on one. It gives no exact construction date.

text: The town has flooded repeatedly, including in 1925, 1932, 1960, 1968, 1979, 2000, 2003, 2013, 2014, 2023 and 2024; November 2024 brought the highest Avon level since local gauging began in 1998. The floodplain narrows from about 600 to 70 metres where the river cuts into town.
source_title: Briefing Note: Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire (community flood briefing)
source_author: Environment Agency with Wiltshire Council, Wessex Water and Bradford on Avon Town Council
uncertainty: The listed years are examples, not a complete record. Earlier floods are not covered, such as the 1882 flood level marked on a plaque shown on the town trail.
